latin.185: GAR. Tum in nomine imputationis peccati varie luditur. § XIX. Nam disputationis initio consenseramus, per imputationis vocem in hoc negotio intelligendum, vel actum judicis declarantis aliquem reum poenaque dignum, vel ipsam poenae inflictionem. Nunc in alia omnia itur. Quaeritur enim, an ipsius Adae actuale peccatum posteris imputetur. Agnoscunt Viri Docti verbotenus; sed explicationem audi: ita scilicet, inquiunt, ut imputari dicatur illa transgressio eodem significatu, quo dixit Apostolus, praeputium imputari in circuncisionem, id est, eodem loco haberi ac si circumcisum esset: Nos enim, ob peccatum nobis ab origine inhaerens, dignos esse, qui eo loco habeamur, ac si actualem ipsam inobedientiam commisissemus. Quod aliquis sane haud immerito tergiversationi deputari debere pretenderit. Convenerat enim, imputare peccatum hoc loco non aliud esse, quam alicui peccatum ita adscribere, ut propter illud, & ejus consideratione reatum subeat, & vel poenas det, vel certe poenis dignus existimetur. At quam remotum sit illud ab eo imputationis significatu, quem hic proponunt, nemo non videt.
latin.186: PLAC. Quod ait me, in nomine imputationis varie lusisse, ab eo longissime abfui, & quam maxime potui serio egi, ut veritatis & pacis decebat studiosum. Abhorrui etiam ab omni tergiversatione, & nihil mihi prius fuit quam ut statum quaestionis purgarem ab omni impedimento, & clarum facerem & liquidum, ne ullus vel tergiversationi, vel dissimulationi, vel declinationi locus esse posset. Quod autem me accusat, quasi conventis non steterim, satis mirari nequeo. Quomodo enim consenseramus Disputationis initio, aut convenerat inter nos de vocis imputationis significatu, qui nunquam ea de re inter nos disputaveramus? Virum enim Doctum mihi nunquam datum est, videre, aut coram alloqui. Ut autem de hac quaestione mecum conferre vellet, impetrare nulla ratione potui. Cum autem dicit, Nunc in alia omnia itur, putas fortasse, Lector, eum hoc meum manufcriptum posterius aut saltem tempus quo scriptum est, designare. At non ita est. Quae enim subjungit verba mea non petuntur ex hoc meo Manufcripto, sed partim ex Thesibus meis de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam, quinquennio, antequam inciperet ista controversia, publicatis, partim ex duarum epistolarum quas solas ad eum scripsi, posteriore, duobus aut tribus a Synodo postrema Nationali mensibus: In priore autem nihil disputabam, tantum ex ipso quaerebam modeste, qua de imputatione Decretum Synodi esset intelligendum, de Mediata, an de Immediata? In posteriore vero breviter ostendebam, nec rationes a me in thesibus allatas mediatam oppugnare imputationem, nec defuisse magnos Theologos qui immediatam negarent confessa mediata. Illud enim utrumque rescripserat ostendendum esse, quod ubi a me factum est, aliquamdiu respondere mihi renuit; tandem vero datis ad me secundis literis protestatus est se mihi ea de re non responsurum, neque mecum aut cum alio ullo eo de negotio disputaturum, nisi in proxima Synodo Nationali. Atque ita finem scribendarum invicem literarum fecimus.
latin.187: Ubi igitur aut quando inter nos ea facta fuerit conventio, diviniare non possum. Fac tamen fuisse factam, quid dixi, quod ei vocis imputationis significatui repugnet? Scripsi in Thesibus supra dictis § VII. Actualem inobedientiam Adami dici posse nobis imputari, hoc sensu, quod ob peccatum nobis ab origine inhaerens digni sumus, qui eodem loco habeamur, ac si inobedientiam illam admisissemus. Est-ne id verum, an falsum? Si falsum, debuit ostendere falsitatem. Si verum, utique non repugnat imputationi mediatae, quam esse veram ipse vir doctus non diffitetur: verum enim vero non repugnat. Imo nihil aliud est quam descriptio imputationis mediatae, quam opposui opinioni Pighii, culpam originis unicam statuentis transgressionem Adami. Cumni, inquit Martyr, nos omnes vult nasci obnoxios, non propter aliquod vitium, aut culpam, aut deprauationem, quam in nobis habeamus. Dixi in Epistola, cum vitium hereditarium nos aeque morte dignos ac Adamum faciat, nihil obstare, quominus peccatum Adami nobis eo sensu dicatur imputari quo dixit Apostolus, si quis legem servaverit, illius praeputium in circuncisionem imputari. Est-ne id verum, nec-ne? Neque ait, neque negat D. Garissolius. Quid igitur facit? eum audi. GAR. Dixerit ergo Paulus, imputari praeputium in circuncisionem, quia eodem loco habeatur ac si circumcisum esset. At hic non de imputatione cujusvis rei agitur, sed de imputatione peccati alieni. Quis autem hactenus vel docuit, vel sibi persuasit, per imputationem illam peccati, intelligendam collationem diversorum peccatorum a diversis personis patratorum, vel paritatem inter diversa peccata ratione poenae aut reatus? Hoc neque Scriptura, neque communis ipse loquendi usus admittit.
latin.188: PLAC. Sumpfine verbum imputandi eo sensu quo illud Paulus sumpsit, cum dixit praeputium imputari in circuncisionem, nec-ne? Non negat Vir doctus. Ergo in eo verbo non lusi, nisi velit in eodem verbo similiter lusisse Apostolum. In ea enim significatione illud usurpavi, cujus gravissimum habeo autorem, ipsum Paulum. At hic, inquit, non de imputatione cujusvis rei agitur, sed de imputatione peccati alieni. Quid tum postea? Est-ne aliquid quod prohibeat illud verbum, quo sensu de alia aliqua re usurpatur, eodem etiam usurpari de peccato? At per imputationem peccati non est intelligenda collatio diversorum peccatorum a diversis personis patratorum vel paritas inter diversa peccata. Quid hoc ad me? An per imputationem inobedientiae Adami talem intellexi vel collationem, vel paritatem? Non certe. Diversa peccata a diversis personis patrata sunt ambo peccata actualia; vitium nobis ab origine inhaerens non est peccatum actuale, sed habituale tantum. Illorum peccatorum diversorum unum non est causa alterius: cum tamen inobedientia actualis nobis inhaerentis habitualis causa fuerit. Itaque conferuntur illa diversa peccata, tanquam ut, ita loquar, coordinata, hae vero inobedientiae tanquam subordinatae. Cum ergo inobedientia Adami sit causa vitii nobis inhaerentis, & hoc sit causa reatus nostri, necesse est inobedientiam Adami causam esse nostri reatus, saltem mediatam. Itaque nos esse reos ob vitium nobis inhaerens immediate, eoque mediante ob inobedientiam illam actualem Adami, cujus vitium illud inhaerens habitualis quaedam est consensus & approbatio, & communio: ut ob eam causam magis proprie nobis in peccatum dici possit imputari, quam praeputium in circuncisionem, ob servata Legis δικαιώματα.
latin.189: Caeterum quod ait in Scriptura nullibi ostendi posse imputationem peccati eo sensu usurpatam, conturbare nos non debet: nam phrasis imputare vel imputari peccatum admodum rara est in Scriptura, nec forte nisi cum negatione adjuncta uspiam occurrit. Considera autem, humanissime Lector, quo sensu phrasis aequipollens ab ipso Domino nostro Jesu Christo usurpata fuerit Matth. 23.34. Propterea ecce ego mitto ad vos Prophetas & sapientes, & scribas, & ex ipsis quosdam trucidabitis & crucifigetis, & ex ipsis aliquos flagellabitis in Synagogis vestris, & persequemini ex urbe in urbem, ut veniat super vos omnis sanguis justus effusus super terram, a sanguine Abel justi usque ad sanguinem Zachariae filii Barachiae, quem occidistis inter templum & altare: hoc est, exponente Luca cap. XI. 50. ut a gente ista requiratur sanguis omnium Prophetarum effusus a jacto mundi fundamento. Quin enim illis verbis significata fuerit imputatio peccati negari nequit. Itaque sic in verba illa commentatus est Calvinus, Tametsi Abel non a Judaeis occisus est, ejus tamen necem ipsis imputat Christus, quia inter ipsos & Cain quaedam erat impietatis cognatio. Facit autem vitiositas inhaerens, ut nobis cum Adamo peccante non qualiscunque cognatio peccati, sed consanguinitas intersit. Imo vitium nostrum inhaerens nihil aliud est quam peccatum Adami secundum habitum in nos propagatum, vel instar pestis aut veneni naturali contagio diffusum. Quid est igitur, cur ob illud vitium nobis imputari dici non possit? Vide ergo, Lector, an me potius hoc loco quam ipsum Dominum, Vir Doctus impugnet.
latin.190: GAR. Denique Socinistae imputationem peccati Adae exerte negant, & agnoscunt tamen nos propter nostrum peccatum eodem loco haberi, ac si Adami actualem inobedientiam commisissemus, quia nimirum imputationem peccati sic explicatam agnoverunt, nullam esse veri nominis imputationem. PLAC. Hic quoque nos traducendi cupido tenebras offudit animo Viri Docti. Ait enim Socinistas agnoscere nos propter nostrum peccatum eodem loco haberi, ac si Adami actualem ipsam inobedientiam commisissemus. Id quod falsum est. Volunt enim nos quidem eodem cum Adamo loco haberi, at non propter peccatum nostrum (peccatum enim ab origine nobis inhaerens nullum agnoscunt) sed quia sumus ab eo procreati, & de liberis idem quod de patre judicium sit. Itaque ab eorum sententia abest nostra toto caelo. Caeterum imputationem peccati Adami Socinus verbis negat, re ponit. Nam si idem sit de filio quod de Patre judicium, & hic judicatur peccator & dignus poena, judicatur etiam poena dignus esse filius: Ille quidem quia ipse peccavit, hic vero quia ejus pater peccavit. Id quod, ipso Viro Docto teste, est peccatum patris filio imputare, & quidem imputatione immediata; quippe cum haereditariam corruptionem neget Socinus, sine qua mediata imputatio esse non potest. Adde quod eadem mors infligitur posteris Adami & Adamo. Ipsa autem poenae inflictio est Viro Docto peccati imputatio. Revera igitur Socinus negat imputationem mediatam quam agnosco; immediatam quam impugno verbotenus tantum negat, re autem ipsa affirmat.
latin.191: GAR. Alio deinde colore hanc posteriorem suam imputationem pingunt, cum addunt, nihil obstare, quominus Adami peccatum nobis imputari dicatur, quatenus vitium nostrum haereditarium habitus est, quem primum actuale peccatum reliquit in Adami anima; deinde inclinatio ad similia peccata; tertio consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum. Haec verba ex secunda, quam ad eum scripseram, epistola Vir Doctus deprompsit: sed de suo addidit voces quatenus, deinde, tertio, dividens ea quae conjunxi, ac ex una ratione tres conficiens praeter mentem meam. Locum ex illa epistola Gallice scripta integrum exscribam. Peccatum Adami dici potest nobis ejus posteris imputari tribus modis. Primo, quia (ut innuit Calvinus, vitium quod ab Adamo in nos defluxit peccatum Adami vocans) intra nos est. Secundo, quia cum vitium haereditarium nos aeque morte aeterna dignos ac Adamum faciat, nihil obstat, quominus peccatum Adami nobis eo sensu dicatur imputari, quo dixit Apostolus, si quis legem servaverit, illius praeputium in circuncisionem imputari, hoc est, eodem loco eum haberi ac si fuisset circumcissus. Tertio, quia corruptio haereditaria est habitus, quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & perversa inclinatio ad simile peccatum; ac proinde consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, nihil video quod impediat, quominus nobis imputari dicatur. Hunc ultimum modum, hanc ultimam rationem, Vir Doctus in tres discerpsit, ac mutat quia in quatenus. Sed eum audiamus. GAR. Ubi primum illud mirari subit, quod imputari agnoscunt peccatum Adae, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Haec enim verba praeferre videntur imputationem ipsius habitualis peccati Adae. Quid autem horridius aut absurdius est, in eo quod dicimus, imputari nobis peccatum Adami actuale, quam quod his verbis fatentur, imputari peccatum habituate? praesertim cum imputatio potius ad actus videatur referenda quam ad habitus?
latin.192: PLAC. Primum non dixi, imputari peccatum Adae, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Tantum dixi, quia corruptio haereditaria est habitus quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & perversa propensio ad ejusmodi peccatum, atque adeo consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, causam me non videre, cur non possit dici nobis imputari, nimirum primum illud peccatum, quod corruptionem, quae haereditaria vocatur, in Adami anima reliquit. Id autem aliud esse non potest quam primum illud Adae peccatum actuale. Aliud enim nullum illam deprauationem in Adami anima reliquit. Vides Lector, me imputationem illam, quam mediatam appello, referre ad peccatum Adae actuale, ac rationem reddere, cur ob haereditariam illam corruptionem dici possit nobis imputari. Sed quandoquidem Vir Doctus probat corruptionem, quatenus in Adami anima fuit, nobis imputari, vide quaeso quid consequatur. Primum illa nostra erit, ut peccatum actuale, per imputationem; hoc enim est illius sententiae consentaneum. Vultne igitur posteros Adami corruptos esse, ut loquitur, interpretative, seu imputative? Deinde, peto an corruptio, quatenus nobis inhaeret, nobis imputetur, necne? Si negas; igitur non est vere peccatum, non peragit nos reos. Si ais; igitur bis corruptio nobis imputatur, semel quatenus fuit in Adamo, iterum quatenus est in nobis. Ita magis rei sumus quam Adamus. Quis hoc credat? Denique peto an corruptio, quatenus haesit in Adamo, imputetur nobis immediate, an mediante corruptione? Si hoc, cur idem non dicitur de peccato actuali? Si illud, Ergo illius corruptionis Adae, nostra corruptio poena est: Cur enim non aeque imputati habitualis poena sit, ac imputati actualis? Si ergo illius imputati poena est, magis punitur in nobis peccatum habituale Adami, quam in ipso Adamo punitum est. In nobis enim, si viro Docto fides habetur, punitur inflictione corruptionis, cum ea poena non fuerit corruptio Adami in Adamo punita. Postremo, Si nobis imputatur corruptio ut fuit in Adamo, vel nobis imputatur simul cum eius peccato actuali, vel ante, aut post illud peccatum. Cur ante aut post illud imputetur, causa dici non potest. Si nobis simul imputatur, etiam simul cum actuali imputata fuit Adamo, cur non enim aeque simul illi ac nobis duo illa eius peccata imputata fuissent? Si ergo simul imputata fuerunt ipsi Adamo, eius corruptio non fuit poena peccati actualis: fuisset enim semetipsa prior: antecedit enim imputatio poenam; & prius imputata fuisset Adamo, quam in eo fuisset. Id quod non obscure contradictionem implicat. Sed pergat.

pass_a.185: GAR. Then in the name of the imputation of sin it is variously played. Section XIX. For at the beginning of the dispute we had agreed that by the voice of imputation in this business was to be understood either the act of a judge declaring someone guilty and worthy of punishment, or the infliction of the punishment itself. Now it is gone into all other things. For it is asked whether Adam's own actual sin is imputed to posterity. The Learned Men acknowledge it verbally; but hear the explanation: namely, they say, so that that transgression is said to be imputed in the same signification in which the Apostle said foreskin is imputed for circumcision, that is, to be held in the same place as if it had been circumcised: For we, on account of the sin inhering in us from the origin, are worthy to be held in that place as if we had committed the actual disobedience itself. Which someone might indeed not undeservedly claim ought to be reckoned to tergiversation. For it had been agreed that to impute sin in this place is nothing other than so to ascribe a sin to someone that on account of it, and by its consideration, he undergo guilt, and either pay punishments or at least be judged worthy of punishments. But how remote that is from that signification of imputation which they here propose, no one does not see.
pass_a.186: PLAC. As to what he says, that I variously played in the name of imputation, I was very far from that, and as much as I could I acted seriously, as became one studious of truth and peace. I also abhorred all tergiversation, and nothing was prior for me than that I should purge the state of the question from every impediment, and make it clear and liquid, lest any place could be for tergiversation or dissimulation or declining. But that he accuses me as if I had not stood by agreements, I cannot wonder enough. For how had we agreed at the beginning of the Dispute, or had it been agreed between us about the signification of the word imputation, who had never disputed between us about that matter? For it was never granted me to see the Learned Man, or to speak with him face to face. And that he would confer with me about this question, I could by no means obtain. But when he says, Now it is gone into all other things, perhaps you think, Reader, that he designates this later manuscript of mine or at least the time when it was written. But it is not so. For the words of mine which he subjoins are not drawn from this Manuscript of mine, but partly from my Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, published five years before this controversy began, partly from the later of the two letters which alone I wrote to him, two or three months after the last National Synod: In the former I was disputing nothing, only asking him modestly in what sense the Synod's Decree on imputation was to be understood, concerning the Mediate, or concerning the Immediate? In the latter truly I briefly showed that neither the reasons brought by me in the theses attack mediate imputation, nor that great Theologians were lacking who denied the immediate while confessing the mediate. For he had written back that both those things were to be shown, which when done by me, for some time he refused to answer me; at last truly, giving me second letters, he protested that he would not answer me about that matter, nor dispute with me or with any other about that business, except in the next National Synod. And so we made an end of writing letters back and forth.
pass_a.187: Where therefore or when that agreement was made between us, I cannot divine. Grant nevertheless that it was made: what did I say that fights against that signification of the word imputation? I wrote in the Theses aforesaid section VII. That Adam's actual disobedience can be said to be imputed to us, in this sense, that on account of the sin inhering in us from the origin we are worthy to be held in the same place as if we had committed that disobedience. Is that true, or false? If false, he ought to have shown the falsity. If true, assuredly it does not fight against mediate imputation, which the learned man himself does not deny to be true: for truth does not fight against truth. Nay it is nothing other than a description of mediate imputation, which I opposed to the opinion of Pighius, who makes the sole guilt of origin to be Adam's transgression. Cumni, says Martyr, he wants us all to be born liable, not on account of any vice or fault or depravation which we have in ourselves. I said in the Epistle, when hereditary vice makes us equally worthy of death as Adam, nothing stands in the way why Adam's sin should not be said to be imputed to us in that sense in which the Apostle said, if anyone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision. Is that true, or not? Neither does D. Garissoles affirm, nor deny. What then does he do? Hear him. GAR. Paul therefore will have said foreskin is imputed for circumcision, because it is held in the same place as if it had been circumcised. But here it is not about the imputation of any thing whatsoever, but about the imputation of another's sin. But who hitherto has taught, or persuaded himself, that by that imputation of sin is to be understood a comparison of diverse sins committed by diverse persons, or a parity among diverse sins by reason of punishment or guilt? This neither Scripture nor the common use of speaking itself admits.
pass_a.188: PLAC. Did I take the word of imputing in that sense in which Paul took it, when he said foreskin is imputed for circumcision, or not? The Learned Man does not deny it. Therefore I did not play in that word, unless he wishes the Apostle likewise to have played in the same word. For I used it in that signification whose most weighty author I have, Paul himself. But here, he says, it is not about the imputation of any thing whatsoever, but about the imputation of another's sin. What then afterward? Is there something that prohibits that word, in which sense it is used of some other thing, from being used also of sin? But by the imputation of sin is not to be understood a comparison of diverse sins by diverse persons or a parity among diverse sins. What is this to me? Did I understand by the imputation of Adam's disobedience such a comparison, or parity? Certainly not. Diverse sins committed by diverse persons are both actual sins; the vice inhering in us from the origin is not an actual sin, but only habitual. Of those diverse sins one is not the cause of the other: whereas yet the actual disobedience was the cause of the habitual inhering in us. Therefore those diverse sins are compared as, so to speak, coordinated, but these disobediences as subordinated. Since therefore Adam's disobedience is the cause of the vice inhering in us, and this is the cause of our guilt, it is necessary that Adam's disobedience be the cause of our guilt, at least mediate. Therefore we are guilty on account of the vice inhering in us immediately, and by that mediating on account of that actual disobedience of Adam, of which that inhering vice is a certain habitual consent and approval and communion: so that for that cause it can more properly be said to be imputed to us unto sin than foreskin unto circumcision, on account of the kept δικαιώματα of the Law.
pass_a.189: But as to what he says, that nowhere in Scripture can the imputation of sin used in that sense be shown, that ought not to disturb us: for the phrase to impute or to be imputed sin is exceedingly rare in Scripture, and perhaps nowhere occurs except with a negation joined. But consider, most humane Reader, in what sense an equivalent phrase was used by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, Matthew 23:34. Therefore behold I send to you Prophets and wise men and scribes, and of them you will kill and crucify some, and of them you will scourge some in your Synagogues, and persecute from city to city, that upon you may come all righteous blood poured out upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar: that is, Luke explaining chapter 11:50, that from that generation may be required the blood of all the Prophets poured out from the foundation of the world. For that by those words the imputation of sin was signified cannot be denied. And so Calvin commented on those words: Although Abel was not killed by the Jews, yet Christ imputes his slaughter to them, because between them and Cain there was a certain kinship of impiety. But the inhering viciousness brings it about that between us and sinning Adam there is not just any kinship of sin, but consanguinity. Nay our inhering vice is nothing other than Adam's sin according to habit propagated into us, or like a plague or poison diffused by natural contagion. What is there therefore why it cannot be said to be imputed to us on account of that vice? See therefore, Reader, whether the Learned Man rather attacks me in this place than the Lord himself.
pass_a.190: GAR. Finally the Socinians expressly deny the imputation of Adam's sin, and yet acknowledge that we on account of our sin are held in the same place as if we had committed Adam's actual disobedience, because to be sure they have acknowledged that the imputation of sin so explained is no imputation of the true name. PLAC. Here too the desire of traducing us has poured darkness on the mind of the Learned Man. For he says the Socinians acknowledge that we on account of our sin are held in the same place as if we had committed Adam's actual disobedience itself. Which is false. For they want us indeed to be held in the same place with Adam, but not on account of our sin (for they acknowledge no sin inhering in us from the origin) but because we were begotten by him, and the same judgment is made of children as of the father. And so our view is away from their opinion by the whole heaven. But as for the rest, Socinus denies the imputation of Adam's sin in words, and posits it in the thing. For if the same judgment is of the son as of the Father, and this one is judged a sinner and worthy of punishment, the son also is judged worthy of punishment: that one indeed because he himself sinned, this one truly because his father sinned. Which, by the Learned Man's own witness, is to impute the father's sin to the son, and indeed by immediate imputation; inasmuch as Socinus denies hereditary corruption, without which mediate imputation cannot be. Add that the same death is inflicted on Adam's posterity and on Adam. But the infliction of punishment itself is for the Learned Man the imputation of sin. In reality therefore Socinus denies the mediate imputation which I acknowledge; the immediate which I impugn he denies only verbally, but in the thing itself he affirms.
pass_a.191: GAR. Then with another color they paint this later imputation of theirs, when they add that nothing stands in the way why Adam's sin should not be said to be imputed to us, inasmuch as our hereditary vice is a habit which the first actual sin left in Adam's soul; then an inclination to similar sins; third a habitual consent to that sin. These words the Learned Man drew from the second letter which I had written to him: but of his own he added the words inasmuch as, then, third, dividing what I had joined, and from one reason making three against my mind. I will copy out entire the place from that letter written in French. Adam's sin can be said to be imputed to us his posterity in three ways. First, because (as Calvin hints, calling the vice which flowed from Adam into us Adam's sin) it is within us. Second, because when hereditary vice makes us equally worthy of eternal death as Adam, nothing stands in the way why Adam's sin should not be said to be imputed to us in that sense in which the Apostle said, if anyone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision, that is, that he is held in the same place as if he had been circumcised. Third, because hereditary corruption is a habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul, and a perverse inclination to a like sin; and therefore a habitual consent to that sin, I see nothing that prevents it from being said to be imputed to us. This last mode, this last reason, the Learned Man has torn into three, and changes it because of inasmuch as. But let us hear him. GAR. Where first that comes to be wondered at, that they acknowledge Adam's sin to be imputed, inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. For these words seem to prefer the imputation of Adam's habitual sin itself. But what is more horrible or absurd, in that we say Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, than that by these words they confess habitual sin is imputed? especially since imputation seems rather to be referred to acts than to habits?
pass_a.192: PLAC. First I did not say Adam's sin is imputed, inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. I only said that because hereditary corruption is a habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul, and a perverse propensity to such a sin, and so a habitual consent to that sin, I do not see a cause why it cannot be said to be imputed to us, namely that first sin which left the corruption called hereditary in Adam's soul. But that cannot be other than that first actual sin of Adam. For no other left that depravation in Adam's soul. You see, Reader, that I refer that imputation which I call mediate to Adam's actual sin, and give a reason why on account of that hereditary corruption it can be said to be imputed to us. But since the Learned Man proves that the corruption, inasmuch as it was in Adam's soul, is imputed to us, see please what follows. First that will be ours, as an actual sin, by imputation; for this is agreeable to his opinion. Does he therefore want Adam's posterity to be corrupt, as he speaks, interpretatively, or imputatively? Next I ask whether the corruption, inasmuch as it inheres in us, is imputed to us, or not? If you deny; then it is not truly sin, it does not make us guilty. If you say yes; then the corruption is imputed to us twice, once inasmuch as it was in Adam, again inasmuch as it is in us. So we are more guilty than Adam. Who would believe this? Finally I ask whether the corruption, inasmuch as it stuck in Adam, is imputed to us immediately, or by corruption mediating? If the latter, why is the same not said of the actual sin? If the former, Therefore our corruption is the punishment of that corruption of Adam: For why should the punishment of the imputed habitual not equally be, as of the imputed actual? If therefore it is the punishment of that imputed one, Adam's habitual sin is punished more in us than it was punished in Adam himself. For in us, if faith is had to the learned man, it is punished by the infliction of corruption, whereas that punishment was not Adam's corruption punished in Adam. Lastly, If the corruption as it was in Adam is imputed to us, either it is imputed to us together with his actual sin, or before, or after that sin. Why it should be imputed before or after that, a cause cannot be said. If it is imputed to us together, it was also imputed to Adam together with the actual—for why would those two sins of his not equally have been imputed together to him and to us? If therefore they were imputed together to Adam himself, his corruption was not the punishment of the actual sin: for it would have been prior to itself: for imputation precedes punishment; and it would have been imputed to Adam before it was in him. Which not obscurely implies a contradiction. But let him go on.

185: Garissoles: Next, people play various games with the very name of imputing sin (§ XIX). At the start of the dispute we had agreed that in this business 'imputation' means either a judge's act declaring someone guilty and worthy of punishment, or the infliction of the punishment itself. Now everything is shifted. The question is whether Adam's own actual sin is imputed to his posterity. The learned men grant it in words—but hear their gloss: that transgression is 'imputed,' they say, in the same sense in which the Apostle said foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26)—that is, counted as if circumcised. So we, because of the sin that inheres in us from birth, are worthy to be treated as if we ourselves had committed that actual disobedience. Someone might fairly call that tergiversation. We had agreed that to impute sin here is nothing but so to ascribe a sin to someone that, for its sake and in view of it, he comes under guilt and either suffers punishment or is at least judged worthy of it. How far their proposed sense is from that meaning, anyone can see.
186: Placeus: He says I played variously with the name of imputation. I was nowhere near that. I treated the matter as seriously as I could, as one who cares for truth and peace. I also shrank from every evasion. My first aim was to clear the state of the question of every obstacle and make it plain and liquid, so that there would be no room left for tergiversation, dissimulation, or side-stepping. That he charges me with breaking agreements I can scarcely believe. How had we 'agreed' at the opening of the Dispute, or settled between us the sense of the word imputation, when we had never disputed that point with each other? I was never allowed even to see the learned man or speak with him face to face, and I could by no means get him to confer with me on this question. When he says 'Now everything is shifted,' you may think, Reader, that he means this later manuscript of mine, or at least the time when it was written. Not so. The words of mine he quotes are not taken from this Manuscript, but partly from my Theses on the state of fallen man before grace—published five years before this controversy began—and partly from the later of the only two letters I wrote him, two or three months after the last National Synod. In the first letter I disputed nothing; I only asked him modestly how the Synod's Decree on imputation was to be understood—of the Mediate, or of the Immediate? In the second I briefly showed that the reasons I had given in the theses do not attack mediate imputation, and that great theologians have not been lacking who deny the immediate while confessing the mediate. He had written back that both points must be shown; when I had done so, he for some time refused to answer; at last, in a second letter, he protested that he would not answer me on the matter, nor dispute it with me or with anyone else, except in the next National Synod. And so we ended writing letters to each other.
187: Where or when, then, that agreement between us was made, I cannot guess. Grant it was made: what did I say that contradicts that sense of the word imputation? I wrote in the Theses just named, § VII, that Adam's actual disobedience can be said to be imputed to us in this sense: because of the sin that inheres in us from birth we are worthy to be held in the same place as if we had committed that disobedience. Is that true or false? If false, he ought to have shown the falsehood. If true, it cannot clash with mediate imputation, which the learned man himself does not deny is true—for truth does not clash with truth. It is nothing but a description of mediate imputation, which I set against Pighius's view that the sole guilt of origin is Adam's transgression. 'Cumni,' says Martyr, 'wants us all born liable—not because of any vice, fault, or depravity we have in ourselves.' I said in the Epistle that when hereditary vice makes us as worthy of death as Adam, nothing prevents Adam's sin from being said to be imputed to us in the sense in which the Apostle said that if someone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26). Is that true or not? D. Garissoles neither affirms nor denies. What does he do, then? Hear him. Garissoles: So Paul will have said foreskin is imputed for circumcision because it is counted as if circumcised. But here we are not dealing with the imputation of any thing whatever, but with the imputation of another's sin. Who has ever taught, or persuaded himself, that by that imputation of sin one must understand a comparison of different sins done by different persons, or a parity among different sins as to punishment or guilt? Neither Scripture nor ordinary speech allows that.
188: Placeus: Did I take 'impute' as Paul took it when he said foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26)—yes or no? The learned man will not deny it. Then I was not gaming the word, unless he wants Paul gaming it too. I used Paul's sense; he is my heaviest warrant. But here, says he, we speak not of imputing just any thing, but of imputing another's sin. So what? May a word used of some other matter not also be used, in that same sense, of sin? He adds that imputing sin must not mean lining up different sins by different persons, or a parity of sins for punishment or guilt. How does that touch me? Did I mean by Adam's-disobedience imputation such a lineup or parity? No. Different persons' different sins are both actual; the vice born into us is not actual but only habitual. Neither of those different sins causes the other—yet Adam's actual disobedience caused the habitual vice in us. So those sins sit side by side (coordinated, if I may say so); these disobediences sit under one another. Adam's disobedience causes our inhering vice; that vice causes our guilt; therefore Adam's disobedience causes our guilt—at least as a mediate cause. We are guilty at once for the vice in us, and through that medium for Adam's actual disobedience—of which the inhering vice is a kind of habitual consent, approval, and share. That is why it may more properly be said imputed to us unto sin than foreskin unto circumcision for the Law's kept δικαιώματα.
189: As for the complaint that Scripture nowhere uses 'imputation of sin' in this sense: that need not unsettle us. The wording 'impute / be imputed' of sin is scarce in Scripture, and may never appear except with a negation. Kind Reader, look instead at the equivalent phrasing our Lord Jesus Christ himself used (Matthew 23:34): he sends prophets, wise men, and scribes; some will be killed and crucified, some scourged in the synagogues and hunted from city to city, so that all the righteous blood shed on earth comes upon that generation—from righteous Abel to Zechariah son of Barachiah, murdered between temple and altar. Luke puts the same point (Luke 11:50): that generation must answer for every prophet's blood shed since the world's foundation. Those words plainly signify sin's imputation. Calvin comments: Abel was not slain by the Jews, yet Christ charges them with his death because a kinship of impiety bound them to Cain. The vice that sticks in us does more still—it sets between us and sinning Adam not a loose kinship of sin but blood-relation. Our inhering vice is Adam's sin under the form of habit poured into us, like plague or poison by natural contagion. Why then may it not be said to be imputed to us for that vice's sake? Ask whether the learned man is striking at me here—or at the Lord himself.
190: Garissoles: Last, the Socinians flatly deny that Adam's sin is imputed, yet still say that because of our own sin we stand where we would stand if we had done Adam's actual disobedience—because they treat that sort of 'imputation' as no real imputation at all. Placeus: Again the urge to blacken us has fogged the learned man's mind. He claims the Socinians admit we are held, because of our sin, as if we had done Adam's actual disobedience. False. They do put us in Adam's place—but not for our sin (they grant no birth-inhering sin). They do it because we were begotten by him, and children get the father's judgment. Heaven and earth lie between that and our view. For the rest: Socinus denies Adam's sin-imputation in speech and installs it in substance. If son and Father share one judgment, and the father is judged a sinner worthy of punishment, the son is judged worthy too—the one for his own sin, the other for his father's. On the learned man's own showing, that imputes the father's sin to the son, and immediately—because Socinus denies hereditary corruption, without which mediate imputation cannot stand. The same death falls on Adam and on his posterity; and for the learned man, inflicting punishment is itself imputing sin. So in fact Socinus denies the mediate imputation I grant, and only verbally denies the immediate imputation I oppose—while affirming it in the deed.
191: Garissoles: They next dress this later imputation in fresh paint: nothing, they say, blocks calling Adam's sin imputed to us inasmuch as our hereditary vice is a habit the first actual sin left in Adam's soul; next, an inclination toward like sins; third, habitual consent to that sin. He lifted those words from my second letter to him—then slipped in of his own 'inasmuch as,' 'next,' and 'third,' carving one joined reason into three against my sense. Here is the whole French-letter place. Adam's sin may be said imputed to us his posterity three ways. First: as Calvin hints (naming Adam's sin the vice that flowed from him into us), it is inside us. Second: hereditary vice makes us as worthy of eternal death as Adam, so nothing stops saying Adam's sin is imputed in the Apostle's sense—if someone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26), i.e. he is counted as circumcised. Third: hereditary corruption is the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul, plus a bent toward a like sin, and so habitual consent to that sin—I see no bar to saying it is imputed to us. That last mode, that last reason, the learned man has shredded into three and warped with 'inasmuch as.' Hear him. Garissoles: First wonder: they grant Adam's sin imputed inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. The wording seems to favor imputing Adam's habitual sin itself. What could be worse—when we speak of imputing Adam's actual sin—than confessing by these words that a habitual sin is imputed? Especially when imputation looks to acts, not habits.
192: Placeus: First, I never said Adam's sin is imputed inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in his soul. My point was only this: hereditary corruption is that habit the first sin left there, plus a bent toward such sin, and so habitual consent to it—and I see no reason we may not say the first sin is imputed to us, namely the sin that left what we call hereditary corruption in Adam's soul. That can only be Adam's first actual sin; nothing else planted that depravity in him. So, Reader: the imputation I name mediate I refer to Adam's actual sin, and I explain why hereditary corruption lets us say it is imputed to us. But if the learned man proves the corruption as it stood in Adam's soul is imputed to us, watch what follows. First, that corruption becomes ours as an actual sin by imputation—his own view requires it. Does he then want Adam's posterity corrupt 'interpretatively' or 'imputatively'? Next: is the corruption as it inheres in us also imputed to us? Deny it, and it is not truly sin and does not make us guilty. Affirm it, and corruption is charged twice—once as it was in Adam, again as it is in us—so we are guiltier than Adam. Who believes that? Last: is Adam-stuck corruption imputed to us immediately, or through corruption as a means? If through a means, why not say the same of the actual sin? If immediately, then our corruption is the punishment of Adam's—for why should an imputed habitual not draw punishment as an imputed actual does? If so, Adam's habitual sin is punished harder in us than it was in him: in us, on his showing, by inflicted corruption, whereas that was not how Adam's own corruption was punished in Adam. Finally, if Adam's-as-was corruption is imputed to us, it comes with his actual sin, or before it, or after. Before or after has no cause. If together with us, it was together with Adam too—else why would those two sins not equally have hit him and us at once? If they hit Adam together, his corruption was not the punishment of the actual: it would be earlier than itself, since imputation precedes punishment, and it would be charged to him before it existed in him. That is open contradiction. But let him go on.
